extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the history, methods, and style of mathematical exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and working-method principles used by the Bourbaki collective for producing the Éléments de mathématique and related publications: highly formal, axiomatic, collectively authored mathematical textbooks and summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: The group's standards for rigour and generality are a main priority for the treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The working method (many drafts, vigorous debate, unanimous agreement) yields a final product which satisfies the group's standards for mathematical rigour. Bourbaki's emphasis on rigour was a reaction to Henri Poincaré's freer, intuition-based style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and abstraction (axiomatic approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat topics in the most abstract, axiomatic terms possible; emphasize generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group resolved to begin in the most abstract, axiomatic terms possible (the 'Abstract Packet'), treating prerequisites from scratch. This leads to presenting material at high generality and abstraction, focusing on mathematical structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimous group agreement before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: No material is deemed fit for publication until the group reaches unanimous agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafts are presented, vigorously debated at conferences, and redrafted; unanimous agreement is required before any material is accepted for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive iterative drafting process
rubrics_metrics.description: A given piece of material may require many drafts over several years before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process can require six or more drafts and has been described as 'Sisyphean'. Some drafts are never developed into completed work; the method is slow but intended to ensure quality and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonal, uniform writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an impersonal writing style to produce text acceptable to the entire group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dieudonné, as scribe, adopted an impersonal writing style (not his own) so final drafts would be acceptable to the whole collective. Individual personal styles are avoided in Bourbaki texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalized language and strict formal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Set mathematics in a formalized language with crystal-clear deductions based on strict formal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki insisted on formalized presentations comparable to Russell and Whitehead's approach; the work uses heavy formal notation and very explicit symbolic definitions (noted examples of extremely long formal definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on mathematical structures as organizing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and use the notion of a mathematical structure to unify and organize mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki promoted 'mathematical structures' as a unifying idea (the 'architecture of mathematics'), applying structure theory across topics to show common features and to solve problems via known structure theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/ foundational ordering of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material so that each statement is established only on the basis of earlier results; maintain logical sequencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first half of the Éléments was numbered sequentially and ordered logically so that a given statement depends only on previously established results. Foundational dependencies determine ordering (e.g., insistence that topological vector spaces appear before integration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal use of illustrations and pictorial representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor a formal presentation in text and formulas and generally avoid illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most final drafts avoided illustrations; an exception (e.g., Lie groups and Lie algebras chapters 4–6) occurred where Armand Borel argued visual learning was important. The general preference is against pictorial representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional use of summary volumes without proofs (Fascicules de résultats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some installments consist only of summaries of results, stated without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volumes referred to as 'Fascicules de résultats' contain summaries of results rather than the usual definitions, proofs, and exercises. The group sometimes published such summary-only volumes as part of the Éléments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective authorship and pseudonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish under the collective pseudonym 'Nicolas Bourbaki' and maintain collective personhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group established the mathematical personhood of their collective pseudonym for publication. Bourbaki maintained secrecy about current membership; authorship and some articles were attributed to Bourbaki to emphasize collective work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor via subcommittees
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign topics to subcommittees responsible for drafting specific material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcommittees write drafts on assigned material, which are then presented and debated at conferences. This organizational structure supports the group's method of producing comprehensive, consistent texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for unity of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Present mathematics as a unified whole (hence 'Éléments de mathématique' in the singular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The singular form 'Mathematic' was intended to connote the unity of mathematics; the treatise is structured so parts serve as a shared foundation for later, more specialized books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of overspecialization; favor transferable methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppose overspecialization and promote methods that identify relevant structures applicable across subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dieudonné and others argued against overspecialization, promoting the axiomatic method as a 'Taylor system' for mathematics: identify structures and apply established knowledge about them to new problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict editorial/publishing practices (sequence, revisions, translations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material may be revised, repackaged, published out of logical order, condensed, or translated; careful editorial control is maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication history shows materials revised for new editions, published chronologically out of logical sequence, grouped or partitioned differently in later volumes, and translated into English—reflecting editorial choices to preserve integrity while adapting format.
